newsitem.title: USA: Florida Supreme Court upholds assisted suicide ban.
newsitem.headline: Florida Supreme Court upholds assisted suicide ban.

text.p: The Florida Supreme Court upheld a state law banning physician-assisted suicide on Thursday, saying the practice was not protected under Florida's constitutional right to privacy.
The 5-1 ruling was made in a case brought by Charles Hall, a 35-year-old man near death from AIDS who has waged a legal battle to allow his physician to help him die.
The ruling came less than three weeks after the U.S. Supreme Court upheld similar bans in two cases, saying states had the right to outlaw doctor-assisted suicides.
Florida's highest court made a distinction that actively assisting in another's death was not the same as allowing someone to refuse medical treatment, which is legal.

Justice Stephen Grimes said in a 23-page opinion: "The assistance sought here is not treatment in the traditional sense of that term. It is an affirmative act designed to cause death -- no matter how well grounded the reasoning behind it."
In dissent, Chief Justice Gerald Kogan said advances in medical science have blurred the distinction between natural and assisted death.

"Medicine has pulled the aperture separating life and death far enough apart to expose a limbo unthinkable 50 years ago," Kogan wrote. "Dying no longer falls into the neat categories our ancestors knew. In today's world, we demean the hard reality of terminal illness to say otherwise."
The court left the door open for the state legislature to allow physician-assisted suicide, taking pains to say that a law legalising the practice would not automatically be unconstitutional.
"We do not hold that a carefully crafted statute authorising assisting suicide would be unconstitutional. Nor do we discount the sincerity and strength of the respondents' convictions," Grimes wrote.
Oregon is the only state that has legalised physician-assisted suicide.

Hall, who contracted AIDS from a blood transfusion and appeared at hearings before the state's highest court in May in his wheelchair, has said he wants to end his life when he chooses, with the help of a physician he trusts.

Dr. Cecil McIver, a soft-spoken 73-year-old from Jupiter, Florida, has agreed to assist Hall if he decides to end his life. If the law is not repealed, McIver could face 15 years in prison for helping Hall.
Two other patients whom McIver also agreed to help have since died during the appeal process.

In January, a state circuit judge in Palm Beach County had granted Hall's request to die with the help of a physcian, citing the state's guarantee of the right to privacy as he struck down a 129-year-old Florida law prohibiting assisted suicide.
But Florida immediately appealed that ruling.
